Al-Hawfi said: it may be a substitute (badal) for the nominative mawla, and yughnī would mean yanfaʿu (avails). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute for the waw in (يُنْصَرُونَ), meaning: none will prevent from the punishment except whom Allah has had mercy on, and al-Hawfi had said this before him.

﴿إنَّهُ هو العَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾: He does not help one who disobeyed Him; the Merciful to whoever obeys Him and to whom He pardons.

(p. 38)

﴿And We had certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment,﴾ ﴿from Pharaoh. Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors.﴾ ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds,﴾ ﴿and We gave them of the signs that contained a clear trial.﴾ ﴿Indeed, these people are saying,﴾ ﴿"There is not but our first death, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ ﴿So bring our forefathers, if you should be truthful.﴾ ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is the appointed time for them all,﴾ ﴿the Day when no close friend will avail another close friend at all, nor will they be aided,﴾ ﴿except those on whom Allah has mercy. Indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 44] ﴿Like murky oil, it boils in the bellies,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 45] ﴿like the boiling of scalding water.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 46] ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of Hellfire.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 47] ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of scalding water.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 48] ﴿Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 49] ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 50] ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 51] ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 52] ﴿wearing fine silk and brocade, facing one another.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 53] ﴿So it will be, and We will marry them to fair women with wide, beautiful eyes.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 54] ﴿They will call therein for every kind of fruit, secure.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 55] ﴿They will not taste therein death, except the first death; and He will protect them from the torment of Hellfire.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 56] ﴿As a bounty from your Lord. That is the great attainment.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 57] ﴿Indeed, We have made it easy in your tongue so that they may remember.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 58] ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 59].

It has been recited مِيقاتَهم in the accusative, as the subject of إنَّ, with the predicate being يَوْمَ الفَصْلِ, meaning: indeed, the Day of Judgment is their appointed time and their recompense. ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُغْنِي مَوْلًى عَنْ مَوْلًى شَيْئًا﴾ encompasses all mawla (close ties, such as kinship, manumission, or allegiance) so that they avail nothing at all, meaning not even a little. (ولا هم يُنْصَرُونَ): plural, because مَوْلًى after the negation is general, so it returned to the meaning, not to the wording.

﴿إلّا مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾: al-Kisa'i said: مَن رَحِمَ is in the accusative as an disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ, an exception not of the same category), meaning: "but whom Allah has had mercy on, no one will be able to avail him of what they need from those whom He has cursed among the created." It was said that it is possible for the exception to be connected (istithnā' muttaṣil), meaning: no close relative avails another close relative, except the believers, for it will be permitted for them to intercede for one another. Al-Hawfi said: it may be a substitute (badal) for the nominative mawla, and yughnī would mean yanfaʿu (avails). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute for the waw in (يُنْصَرُونَ), meaning: none will prevent from the punishment except whom Allah has had mercy on, and al-Hawfi had said this before him.

﴿إنَّهُ هو العَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾: He does not help one who disobeyed Him; the Merciful to whoever obeys Him and to whom He pardons.

(p. 38)

﴿And We had certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment,﴾ ﴿from Pharaoh. Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors.﴾ ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds,﴾ ﴿and We gave them of the signs that contained a clear trial.﴾ ﴿Indeed, these people are saying,﴾ ﴿"There is not but our first death, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ ﴿So bring our forefathers, if you should be truthful.﴾ ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is the appointed time for them all,﴾ ﴿the Day when no close friend will avail another close friend at all, nor will they be aided,﴾ ﴿except those on whom Allah has mercy. Indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 44] ﴿Like murky oil, it boils in the bellies,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 45] ﴿like the boiling of scalding water.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 46] ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of Hellfire.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 47] ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of scalding water.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 48] ﴿Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 49] ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 50] ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 51] ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 52] ﴿wearing fine silk and brocade, facing one another.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 53] ﴿So it will be, and We will marry them to fair women with wide, beautiful eyes.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 54] ﴿They will call therein for every kind of fruit, secure.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 55] ﴿They will not taste therein death, except the first death; and He will protect them from the torment of Hellfire.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 56] ﴿As a bounty from your Lord. That is the great attainment.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 57] ﴿Indeed, We have made it easy in your tongue so that they may remember.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 58] ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 59].

When the Most High mentioned the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, He mentioned His favour to the Children of Israel, beginning with the averting of harm from them, which was their deliverance from the torment they had been in. Then He mentioned the continuing benefit to them, from His choosing them over the worlds and His giving them the signs. The humiliating torment was the killing of their sons and their employment in arduous labour. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ as ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ [the attributive construction], which is an idafa of the noun to its adjective, like بَقْلَةِ الحَمْقاءِ (the foolish herb, i.e., purslane). And ﴿مِن فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ is a substitute (badal, appositive substitute) for (مِنَ العَذابِ), with an omitted modifier, meaning "from the torment of Pharaoh." Then the modifier was omitted, and Pharaoh himself was made the torment, as hyperbole (mubalaghah). It was also said: it is connected to an omitted word, meaning "existing and proceeding from Pharaoh." Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿مَن فِرْعَوْنُ﴾ (who is Pharaoh?). مَن is an interrogative: a subject (mubtada'), and فِرْعَوْنُ is its predicate. When He described Pharaoh with severity and atrocity, He said: "Who is Pharaoh?", meaning: do you know him, who he is in his arrogance and rebellion? Then He made his state in that clear by saying ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ عالِيًا مِنَ المُسْرِفِينَ﴾ (Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors), meaning: exalted over the world, or arrogant, a transgressor among the transgressors.

﴿ولَقَدِ اخْتَرْناهُمْ﴾ means: We chose them and honoured them. (عَلى عِلْمٍ) — عِلْمٍ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) whose agent is not mentioned. It was said: "knowingly on their part and with excellence in them, so We chose them for prophethoods and messengerships." It was also said: "knowingly on Our part," meaning knowing the place of choice and that they deserved to be chosen. It was also said: "knowingly on Our part of what would proceed from them of justice, goodness, knowledge and faith, and that they would go astray and commit lapses in some matters."

(p. 38) It was also said: We chose them through this deliverance and these blessings, on account of prior knowledge We had of them, and We singled them out for that over the worlds. (عَلى العالَمِينَ): meaning the worlds of their own time, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to them. It was also said: "over the worlds" is general because of the large number of prophets among them, while this is specific to them and not to others. The choosing was from this aspect, since the community of Muhammad is superior. The word عَلى in His saying (عَلى عِلْمٍ) does not have the same meaning as عَلى in His saying (عَلى العالَمِينَ), and for this reason both were attached to a single verb, since the meaning differed, as in the poet's verse:

"And one day upon the back of the sand dune she became unattainable to me, and swore an oath that was not qualified."

So عَلى عِلْمٍ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), either from the agent or from the object. And عَلى ظَهْرِ is a circumstantial clause from the agent in تَعَذَّرَتْ, and the governing element (al-ʿāmil) of the one who has the circumstance is the verb.

﴿وآتَيْناهم مِنَ الآياتِ﴾ means: the manifest miracles among the people of Pharaoh, and what they were afflicted with, and among the Children of Israel what He bestowed upon them of shading by the clouds, manna and quails, and other things that He did not manifest to others.

﴿ما فِيهِ بَلاءٌ﴾ means: a clear test with blessings, or the trial through blessings, like His saying: ﴿ونَبْلُوكم بِالشَّرِّ والخَيْرِ﴾ (And We test you with evil and good) [al-Anbiya': 35]. (إنَّ هَؤُلاءِ): meaning the Quraysh, and in the demonstrative there is belittling of them.

﴿لَيَقُولُونَ﴾ ﴿إنْ هي إلّا مَوْتَتُنا الأُولى﴾ means: death is confined to our first death. He had said: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكم ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكم ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكُمْ﴾ (You were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life) [al-Baqarah: 28], mentioning two deaths, a first and a second. They denied that there would be a second death for them. The meaning is: the end of our affair and the limit of our existence is only at our death. Thus their statement implies the denial of resurrection. Then they stated explicitly what their statement implied, saying: ﴿وما نَحْنُ بِمُنْشَرِينَ﴾ (and we will not be resurrected), meaning: we will not be raised to everlasting life in which there is reckoning, reward and punishment. Their saying was in the sense of their saying: ﴿إنْ هي إلّا حَياتُنا الدُّنْيا وما نَحْنُ بِمَبْعُوثِينَ﴾ (There is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected) [al-An'am: 29].

﴿فَأْتُوا بِآبائِنا﴾: an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to the believers who were promising them resurrection, meaning: if you are truthful in what you say, then revive for us those of our sons who died, by asking your Lord, so that this would be a proof of resurrection in the Hereafter. It was said: they asked the Messenger to supplicate to Allah so that He would revive for them Quṣayy ibn Kilab, that they might consult him concerning the truth of prophethood and resurrection, since he was their elder and their consultant in calamities. (أهم): meaning the Quraysh, ﴿خَيْرٌ أمْ قَوْمُ تُبَّعٍ﴾? Apparently Tubba' is a well-known person, and comparison was made between his people and the people of the Messenger (ﷺ). Although the word Tubba' is applied to everyone who ruled the Arabs, just as Kisra is applied to whoever ruled Persia and Caesar to whoever ruled Rome. It was said: his name was As'ad al-Himyari, and he was called Abu Karib. Abu Hatim al-Riyashi mentioned that he believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) seven hundred years before he was sent. It is reported that when he believed in Medina, he wrote a letter and composed poetry. As for the poetry, it is:

"I bear witness concerning Ahmad that he is a messenger from Allah, Creator of souls."

"If my life were extended to his life, I would be his minister and his cousin."

As for the letter, Ibn Ishaq and others reported that it contained: "To proceed: I have believed in you and in the Book that was revealed to you, and I am upon your religion and your practice. I have believed in your Lord and the Lord of everything, and I have believed in everything that came from your Lord of the laws of Islam. If I attain you, then so be it, and how excellent; and if I do not attain you, then intercede for me and do not forget me on the Day of Resurrection, for I am of your first community. I followed you before your coming, and I am upon your creed and the creed of your father Abraham (peace be upon him)." Then he sealed the letter and engraved upon it: "To Allah belongs the command, before and after." He wrote its address: "To Muhammad son of ʿAbd Allah, the Prophet of Allah and His Messenger, the Seal of the Prophets, and the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds (ﷺ), from Tubba' the First." It is said that the letter and the poetry were with Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd, and they remained with him until the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, and they had been inheriting them generation after generation until they delivered them to the Prophet (ﷺ).

From Ibn ʿAbbas: Tubba' was a prophet. And from him: when Tubba' came from the East, after he had overcome al-Hira and Samarqand, he headed for Medina, having left behind some of his people there when he traveled, and they were killed by stealth, so he resolved to destroy it and exterminate its people. They gathered the Ansar for him and went out to fight him, and they would fight him by day and host him by night. This pleased him and he said: "Indeed, these people are noble." Then Ka'b and Asad, two cousins of Qurayzah, neighbours, came to him and informed him that "it will be prevented between you and what you want, for it is the migration place of a prophet from Quraysh named Muhammad, and his birthplace is in Mecca." Their statement turned him away from what he intended. Then they invited him to their religion, and he followed them and honoured them. They departed from Medina, and with them a group of Jews. On the way, a group from Hudhayl said to him: "We will guide you to a house in Mecca in which there is a treasure of pearls, chrysolite and silver." Hudhayl wanted his destruction, because they knew that no one who intended him harm would fail to perish. He mentioned this to the two rabbis, and they said: "We do not know of any house for Allah on earth other than this one. Take it as a place of worship, perform your sacrifice there, and shave your head. The people only intended your destruction." So he honoured it and covered it with cloth, and he was the first to clothe the House. He cut off the hands and feet of those men from Hudhayl, put out their eyes, and crucified them.

Some people said: by Tubba' is not meant a single man, but rather the kings of Yemen, who were called the Tababi'ah (tubba'ah). What appears is that he meant one of these, whom the Arabs know by this name more than others know it. In a hadith: "Do not revile Tubba', for he was a believer." This indicates that he is one specific person. Al-Jawhari said: the Tababi'ah are the kings of Yemen; and al-tubbaʿ is the shadow; and al-tubbaʿ is a kind of bird. Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli said: Tubba' is the title of every king of Yemen, al-Shihr and Hadramawt, and the king of Yemen alone is not called Tubba', as al-Mas'udi said. The comparison in which superiority is claimed concerns two categories, neither of which has goodness in them, relative to strength and power, as He said: ﴿أكُفّارُكم خَيْرٌ مِن أُولَئِكُمْ﴾ (Are your disbelievers better than those?) [al-Qamar: 43]. In Ibn ʿAbbas's exegesis, after mentioning the family of Pharaoh: "Are they stronger, or the people of Tubba'?" The attribution of "people" (qawm) to Tubba' is evidence that his creed was not theirs.

﴿أهْلَكْناهم إنَّهم كانُوا مُجْرِمِينَ﴾: a report of what He did to them, and an alert that the cause of destruction is criminality. In this there is a warning to the Quraysh and a threat that He may do to them what He did to the people of Tubba' and those before them, the deniers of the messengers, for their criminality. Then He mentioned the decisive proof of the correctness of the doctrine of resurrection, which is the creation of the world in truth. Most readers recite (وما بَيْنَهُما) with the masculine dual, but Ubayd ibn ʿUmayr read: (وما بَيْنَهُنَّ لاعِبِينَ). Muqatil said: "playing" means "frivolous."

It was said: they asked the Messenger to supplicate to Allah so that He would revive for them Quṣayy ibn Kilab, that they might consult him concerning the truth of prophethood and resurrection, since he was their elder and their consultant in calamities. (أهم): meaning the Quraysh, ﴿خَيْرٌ أمْ قَوْمُ تُبَّعٍ﴾? Apparently Tubba' is a well-known person, and comparison was made between his people and the people of the Messenger (ﷺ). Although the word Tubba' is applied to everyone who ruled the Arabs, just as Kisra is applied to whoever ruled Persia and Caesar to whoever ruled Rome. It was said: his name was As'ad al-Himyari, and he was called Abu Karib. Abu Hatim al-Riyashi mentioned that he believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) seven hundred years before he was sent. "I bear witness concerning Ahmad that he is a messenger from Allah, Creator of souls."

"If my life were extended to his life, I would be his minister and his cousin."

As for the letter, Ibn Ishaq and others reported that it contained: "To proceed: I have believed in you and in the Book that was revealed to you, and I am upon your religion and your practice. I have believed in your Lord and the Lord of everything, and I have believed in everything that came from your Lord of the laws of Islam. If I attain you, then so be it, and how excellent; and if I do not attain you, then intercede for me and do not forget me on the Day of Resurrection, for I am of your first community. I followed you before your coming, and I am upon your creed and the creed of your father Abraham (peace be upon him)." Then he sealed the letter and engraved upon it: "To Allah belongs the command, before and after." It is said that the letter and the poetry were with Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd, and they remained with him until the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, and they had been inheriting them generation after generation until they delivered them to the Prophet (ﷺ).

They gathered the Ansar for him and went out to fight him, and they would fight him by day and host him by night. This pleased him and he said: "Indeed, these people are noble." (ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ): that He created that, so they do not fear punishment nor hope for reward. When the Most High mentioned the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, He mentioned His favour to the Children of Israel, beginning with the averting of harm from them, which was their deliverance from the torment they had been in. Then He mentioned the continuing benefit to them, from His choosing them over the worlds and His giving them the signs. The humiliating torment was the killing of their sons and their employment in arduous labour. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ as ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ [the attributive construction], which is an idafa of the noun to its adjective, like بَقْلَةِ الحَمْقاءِ (the foolish herb, i.e., purslane). And ﴿مِن فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ is a substitute (badal, appositive substitute) for (مِنَ العَذابِ), with an omitted modifier, meaning "from the torment of Pharaoh." Then the modifier was omitted, and Pharaoh himself was made the torment, as hyperbole (mubalaghah). It was also said: it is connected to an omitted word, meaning "existing and proceeding from Pharaoh." Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿مَن فِرْعَوْنُ﴾ (who is Pharaoh?). مَن is an interrogative: a subject (mubtada'), and فِرْعَوْنُ is its predicate. When He described Pharaoh with severity and atrocity, He said: "Who is Pharaoh?", meaning: do you know him, who he is in his arrogance and rebellion? Then He made his state in that clear by saying ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ عالِيًا مِنَ المُسْرِفِينَ﴾ (Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors), meaning: exalted over the world, or arrogant, a transgressor among the transgressors.

﴿ولَقَدِ اخْتَرْناهُمْ﴾ means: We chose them and honoured them. (عَلى عِلْمٍ) — عِلْمٍ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) whose agent is not mentioned. It was said: "knowingly on their part and with excellence in them, so We chose them for prophethoods and messengerships." It was also said: "knowingly on Our part," meaning knowing the place of choice and that they deserved to be chosen. It was also said: "knowingly on Our part of what would proceed from them of justice, goodness, knowledge and faith, and that they would go astray and commit lapses in some matters."

(p. 38) It was also said: We chose them through this deliverance and these blessings, on account of prior knowledge We had of them, and We singled them out for that over the worlds. (عَلى العالَمِينَ): meaning the worlds of their own time, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to them. It was also said: "over the worlds" is general because of the large number of prophets among them, while this is specific to them and not to others. The choosing was from this aspect, since the community of Muhammad is superior. The word عَلى in His saying (عَلى عِلْمٍ) does not have the same meaning as عَلى in His saying (عَلى العالَمِينَ), and for this reason both were attached to a single verb, since the meaning differed, as in the poet's verse:

"And one day upon the back of the sand dune she became unattainable to me, and swore an oath that was not qualified."

So عَلى عِلْمٍ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), either from the agent or from the object. And عَلى ظَهْرِ is a circumstantial clause from the agent in تَعَذَّرَتْ, and the governing element (al-ʿāmil) of the one who has the circumstance is the verb.

When the Most High mentioned the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, He mentioned His favour to the Children of Israel, beginning with the averting of harm from them, which was their deliverance from the torment they had been in. Then He mentioned the continuing benefit to them, from His choosing them over the worlds and His giving them the signs. The humiliating torment was the killing of their sons and their employment in arduous labour. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ as ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ [the attributive construction], which is an idafa of the noun to its adjective, like بَقْلَةِ الحَمْقاءِ (the foolish herb, i.e., purslane). And ﴿مِن فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ is a substitute (badal, appositive substitute) for (مِنَ العَذابِ), with an omitted modifier, meaning "from the torment of Pharaoh." Then the modifier was omitted, and Pharaoh himself was made the torment, as hyperbole (mubalaghah). Then He made his state in that clear by saying ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ عالِيًا مِنَ المُسْرِفِينَ﴾ (Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors), meaning: exalted over the world, or arrogant, a transgressor among the transgressors.

﴿ولَقَدِ اخْتَرْناهُمْ﴾ means: We chose them and honoured them. (عَلى عِلْمٍ) — عِلْمٍ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) whose agent is not mentioned. It was said: "knowingly on their part and with excellence in them, so We chose them for prophethoods and messengerships." It was also said: "knowingly on Our part," meaning knowing the place of choice and that they deserved to be chosen. It was also said: "knowingly on Our part of what would proceed from them of justice, goodness, knowledge and faith, and that they would go astray and commit lapses in some matters."

(p. 38) It was also said: We chose them through this deliverance and these blessings, on account of prior knowledge We had of them, and We singled them out for that over the worlds. (عَلى العالَمِينَ): meaning the worlds of their own time, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to them. It was also said: "over the worlds" is general because of the large number of prophets among them, while this is specific to them and not to others. The choosing was from this aspect, since the community of Muhammad is superior. The word عَلى in His saying (عَلى عِلْمٍ) does not have the same meaning as عَلى in His saying (عَلى العالَمِينَ), and for this reason both were attached to a single verb, since the meaning differed, as in the poet's verse:

"And one day upon the back of the sand dune she became unattainable to me, and swore an oath that was not qualified."

﴿وآتَيْناهم مِنَ الآياتِ﴾ means: the manifest miracles among the people of Pharaoh, and what they were afflicted with, and among the Children of Israel what He bestowed upon them of shading by the clouds, manna and quails, and other things that He did not manifest to others.

﴿ما فِيهِ بَلاءٌ﴾ means: a clear test with blessings, or the trial through blessings, like His saying: ﴿ونَبْلُوكم بِالشَّرِّ والخَيْرِ﴾ (And We test you with evil and good) [al-Anbiya': 35]. (إنَّ هَؤُلاءِ): meaning the Quraysh, and in the demonstrative there is belittling of them.

﴿لَيَقُولُونَ﴾ ﴿إنْ هي إلّا مَوْتَتُنا الأُولى﴾ means: death is confined to our first death. He had said: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكم ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكم ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكُمْ﴾ (You were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life) [al-Baqarah: 28], mentioning two deaths, a first and a second. They denied that there would be a second death for them. The meaning is: the end of our affair and the limit of our existence is only at our death. Thus their statement implies the denial of resurrection. Then they stated explicitly what their statement implied, saying: ﴿وما نَحْنُ بِمُنْشَرِينَ﴾ (and we will not be resurrected), meaning: we will not be raised to everlasting life in which there is reckoning, reward and punishment. Their saying was in the sense of their saying: ﴿إنْ هي إلّا حَياتُنا الدُّنْيا وما نَحْنُ بِمَبْعُوثِينَ﴾ (There is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected) [al-An'am: 29].

﴿فَأْتُوا بِآبائِنا﴾: an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to the believers who were promising them resurrection, meaning: if you are truthful in what you say, then revive for us those of our sons who died, by asking your Lord, so that this would be a proof of resurrection in the Hereafter. It was said: they asked the Messenger to supplicate to Allah so that He would revive for them Quṣayy ibn Kilab, that they might consult him concerning the truth of prophethood and resurrection, since he was their elder and their consultant in calamities. (أهم): meaning the Quraysh, ﴿خَيْرٌ أمْ قَوْمُ تُبَّعٍ﴾? Apparently Tubba' is a well-known person, and comparison was made between his people and the people of the Messenger (ﷺ). Although the word Tubba' is applied to everyone who ruled the Arabs, just as Kisra is applied to whoever ruled Persia and Caesar to whoever ruled Rome. It was said: his name was As'ad al-Himyari, and he was called Abu Karib. Abu Hatim al-Riyashi mentioned that he believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) seven hundred years before he was sent. It is reported that when he believed in Medina, he wrote a letter and composed poetry. As for the poetry, it is:

"I bear witness concerning Ahmad that he is a messenger from Allah, Creator of souls."

"If my life were extended to his life, I would be his minister and his cousin."

As for the letter, Ibn Ishaq and others reported that it contained: "To proceed: I have believed in you and in the Book that was revealed to you, and I am upon your religion and your practice. I have believed in your Lord and the Lord of everything, and I have believed in everything that came from your Lord of the laws of Islam. If I attain you, then so be it, and how excellent; and if I do not attain you, then intercede for me and do not forget me on the Day of Resurrection, for I am of your first community. I followed you before your coming, and I am upon your creed and the creed of your father Abraham (peace be upon him)." Then he sealed the letter and engraved upon it: "To Allah belongs the command, before and after." He wrote its address: "To Muhammad son of ʿAbd Allah, the Prophet of Allah and His Messenger, the Seal of the Prophets, and the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds (ﷺ), from Tubba' the First." It is said that the letter and the poetry were with Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd, and they remained with him until the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, and they had been inheriting them generation after generation until they delivered them to the Prophet (ﷺ).

From Ibn ʿAbbas: Tubba' was a prophet. And from him: when Tubba' came from the East, after he had overcome al-Hira and Samarqand, he headed for Medina, having left behind some of his people there when he traveled, and they were killed by stealth, so he resolved to destroy it and exterminate its people. They gathered the Ansar for him and went out to fight him, and they would fight him by day and host him by night. This pleased him and he said: "Indeed, these people are noble." Then Ka'b and Asad, two cousins of Qurayzah, neighbours, came to him and informed him that "it will be prevented between you and what you want, for it is the migration place of a prophet from Quraysh named Muhammad, and his birthplace is in Mecca." Their statement turned him away from what he intended. Then they invited him to their religion, and he followed them and honoured them. They departed from Medina, and with them a group of Jews. On the way, a group from Hudhayl said to him: "We will guide you to a house in Mecca in which there is a treasure of pearls, chrysolite and silver." Hudhayl wanted his destruction, because they knew that no one who intended him harm would fail to perish. He mentioned this to the two rabbis, and they said: "We do not know of any house for Allah on earth other than this one. Take it as a place of worship, perform your sacrifice there, and shave your head. The people only intended your destruction." So he honoured it and covered it with cloth, and he was the first to clothe the House. He cut off the hands and feet of those men from Hudhayl, put out their eyes, and crucified them.

Some people said: by Tubba' is not meant a single man, but rather the kings of Yemen, who were called the Tababi'ah (tubba'ah). What appears is that he meant one of these, whom the Arabs know by this name more than others know it. In a hadith: "Do not revile Tubba', for he was a believer." This indicates that he is one specific person. Al-Jawhari said: the Tababi'ah are the kings of Yemen; and al-tubbaʿ is the shadow; and al-tubbaʿ is a kind of bird. Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli said: Tubba' is the title of every king of Yemen, al-Shihr and Hadramawt, and the king of Yemen alone is not called Tubba', as al-Mas'udi said. The comparison in which superiority is claimed concerns two categories, neither of which has goodness in them, relative to strength and power, as He said: ﴿أكُفّارُكم خَيْرٌ مِن أُولَئِكُمْ﴾ (Are your disbelievers better than those?) The attribution of "people" (qawm) to Tubba' is evidence that his creed was not theirs.

In this there is a warning to the Quraysh and a threat that He may do to them what He did to the people of Tubba' and those before them, the deniers of the messengers, for their criminality. Then He mentioned the decisive proof of the correctness of the doctrine of resurrection, which is the creation of the world in truth. Most readers recite (وما بَيْنَهُما) with the masculine dual, but Ubayd ibn ʿUmayr read: (وما بَيْنَهُنَّ لاعِبِينَ). Muqatil said: "playing" means "frivolous."

﴿ما خَلَقْناهُما إلّا بِالحَقِّ﴾ means: with justice, rewarding the doer of good and the doer of evil with the reward and punishment He wills. It has been recited مِيقاتَهم in the accusative, as the subject of إنَّ, with the predicate being يَوْمَ الفَصْلِ, meaning: indeed, the Day of Judgment is their appointed time and their recompense. ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُغْنِي مَوْلًى عَنْ مَوْلًى شَيْئًا﴾ encompasses all mawla (close ties, such as kinship, manumission, or allegiance) so that they avail nothing at all, meaning not even a little. ﴿إلّا مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾: al-Kisa'i said: مَن رَحِمَ is in the accusative as an disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ, an exception not of the same category), meaning: "but whom Allah has had mercy on, no one will be able to avail him of what they need from those whom He has cursed among the created." It was said that it is possible for the exception to be connected (istithnā' muttaṣil), meaning: no close relative avails another close relative, except the believers, for it will be permitted for them to intercede for one another. Al-Hawfi said: it may be a substitute (badal) for the nominative mawla, and yughnī would mean yanfaʿu (avails). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute for the waw in (يُنْصَرُونَ), meaning: none will prevent from the punishment except whom Allah has had mercy on, and al-Hawfi had said this before him.

﴿إنَّهُ هو العَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾: He does not help one who disobeyed Him; the Merciful to whoever obeys Him and to whom He pardons.

(p. 38)

[al-Qamar: 43]. In Ibn ʿAbbas's exegesis, after mentioning the family of Pharaoh: "Are they stronger, or the people of Tubba'?" In this there is a warning to the Quraysh and a threat that He may do to them what He did to the people of Tubba' and those before them, the deniers of the messengers, for their criminality. Most readers recite (وما بَيْنَهُما) with the masculine dual, but Ubayd ibn ʿUmayr read: (وما بَيْنَهُنَّ لاعِبِينَ). Muqatil said: "playing" means "frivolous."

﴿And We had certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment,﴾ ﴿from Pharaoh. That is the great attainment.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 57] ﴿Indeed, We have made it easy in your tongue so that they may remember.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 58] ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 59].

Then He made his state in that clear by saying ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ عالِيًا مِنَ المُسْرِفِينَ﴾ (Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors), meaning: exalted over the world, or arrogant, a transgressor among the transgressors.

﴿ولَقَدِ اخْتَرْناهُمْ﴾ means: We chose them and honoured them. (عَلى عِلْمٍ) — عِلْمٍ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) whose agent is not mentioned. It was said: "knowingly on their part and with excellence in them, so We chose them for prophethoods and messengerships." It was also said: "knowingly on Our part," meaning knowing the place of choice and that they deserved to be chosen. It was also said: "knowingly on Our part of what would proceed from them of justice, goodness, knowledge and faith, and that they would go astray and commit lapses in some matters."

(p. 38) It was also said: We chose them through this deliverance and these blessings, on account of prior knowledge We had of them, and We singled them out for that over the worlds. (عَلى العالَمِينَ): meaning the worlds of their own time, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to them. It was also said: "over the worlds" is general because of the large number of prophets among them, while this is specific to them and not to others. The choosing was from this aspect, since the community of Muhammad is superior. ﴿لَيَقُولُونَ﴾ ﴿إنْ هي إلّا مَوْتَتُنا الأُولى﴾ means: death is confined to our first death. They denied that there would be a second death for them. The meaning is: the end of our affair and the limit of our existence is only at our death. It was said: they asked the Messenger to supplicate to Allah so that He would revive for them Quṣayy ibn Kilab, that they might consult him concerning the truth of prophethood and resurrection, since he was their elder and their consultant in calamities. (أهم): meaning the Quraysh, ﴿خَيْرٌ أمْ قَوْمُ تُبَّعٍ﴾? Apparently Tubba' is a well-known person, and comparison was made between his people and the people of the Messenger (ﷺ). Although the word Tubba' is applied to everyone who ruled the Arabs, just as Kisra is applied to whoever ruled Persia and Caesar to whoever ruled Rome. It was said: his name was As'ad al-Himyari, and he was called Abu Karib. Abu Hatim al-Riyashi mentioned that he believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) seven hundred years before he was sent. It is reported that when he believed in Medina, he wrote a letter and composed poetry. As for the poetry, it is:

"I bear witness concerning Ahmad that he is a messenger from Allah, Creator of souls."

"If my life were extended to his life, I would be his minister and his cousin."

As for the letter, Ibn Ishaq and others reported that it contained: "To proceed: I have believed in you and in the Book that was revealed to you, and I am upon your religion and your practice. I have believed in your Lord and the Lord of everything, and I have believed in everything that came from your Lord of the laws of Islam. If I attain you, then so be it, and how excellent; and if I do not attain you, then intercede for me and do not forget me on the Day of Resurrection, for I am of your first community. I followed you before your coming, and I am upon your creed and the creed of your father Abraham (peace be upon him)." Then he sealed the letter and engraved upon it: "To Allah belongs the command, before and after." He wrote its address: "To Muhammad son of ʿAbd Allah, the Prophet of Allah and His Messenger, the Seal of the Prophets, and the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds (ﷺ), from Tubba' the First." It is said that the letter and the poetry were with Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd, and they remained with him until the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, and they had been inheriting them generation after generation until they delivered them to the Prophet (ﷺ).

From Ibn ʿAbbas: Tubba' was a prophet. And from him: when Tubba' came from the East, after he had overcome al-Hira and Samarqand, he headed for Medina, having left behind some of his people there when he traveled, and they were killed by stealth, so he resolved to destroy it and exterminate its people. They gathered the Ansar for him and went out to fight him, and they would fight him by day and host him by night. This pleased him and he said: "Indeed, these people are noble." Then Ka'b and Asad, two cousins of Qurayzah, neighbours, came to him and informed him that "it will be prevented between you and what you want, for it is the migration place of a prophet from Quraysh named Muhammad, and his birthplace is in Mecca." On the way, a group from Hudhayl said to him: "We will guide you to a house in Mecca in which there is a treasure of pearls, chrysolite and silver." He mentioned this to the two rabbis, and they said: "We do not know of any house for Allah on earth other than this one. ﴿ما فِيهِ بَلاءٌ﴾ means: a clear test with blessings, or the trial through blessings, like His saying: ﴿ونَبْلُوكم بِالشَّرِّ والخَيْرِ﴾ (And We test you with evil and good) [al-Anbiya': 35]. (إنَّ هَؤُلاءِ): meaning the Quraysh, and in the demonstrative there is belittling of them.

﴿لَيَقُولُونَ﴾ ﴿إنْ هي إلّا مَوْتَتُنا الأُولى﴾ means: death is confined to our first death. He had said: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكم ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكم ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكُمْ﴾ (You were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life) [al-Baqarah: 28], mentioning two deaths, a first and a second. Then they stated explicitly what their statement implied, saying: ﴿وما نَحْنُ بِمُنْشَرِينَ﴾ (and we will not be resurrected), meaning: we will not be raised to everlasting life in which there is reckoning, reward and punishment. Then He mentioned the continuing benefit to them, from His choosing them over the worlds and His giving them the signs. The humiliating torment was the killing of their sons and their employment in arduous labour. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ as ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ [the attributive construction], which is an idafa of the noun to its adjective, like بَقْلَةِ الحَمْقاءِ (the foolish herb, i.e., purslane). Then the modifier was omitted, and Pharaoh himself was made the torment, as hyperbole (mubalaghah). It was also said: it is connected to an omitted word, meaning "existing and proceeding from Pharaoh." When He described Pharaoh with severity and atrocity, He said: "Who is Pharaoh?", meaning: do you know him, who he is in his arrogance and rebellion? Then He made his state in that clear by saying ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ عالِيًا مِنَ المُسْرِفِينَ﴾ (Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors), meaning: exalted over the world, or arrogant, a transgressor among the transgressors.

It was said: "knowingly on their part and with excellence in them, so We chose them for prophethoods and messengerships." It was also said: "knowingly on Our part," meaning knowing the place of choice and that they deserved to be chosen. It was also said: "knowingly on Our part of what would proceed from them of justice, goodness, knowledge and faith, and that they would go astray and commit lapses in some matters."

(p. 38) It was also said: We chose them through this deliverance and these blessings, on account of prior knowledge We had of them, and We singled them out for that over the worlds. It was also said: "over the worlds" is general because of the large number of prophets among them, while this is specific to them and not to others. The choosing was from this aspect, since the community of Muhammad is superior. We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is the appointed time for them all,﴾ ﴿the Day when no close friend will avail another close friend at all, nor will they be aided,﴾ ﴿except those on whom Allah has mercy. Indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 44] ﴿Like murky oil, it boils in the bellies,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 45] ﴿like the boiling of scalding water.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 46] ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of Hellfire.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 47] ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of scalding water.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 48] ﴿Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 49] ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 50] ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 51] ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 52] ﴿wearing fine silk and brocade, facing one another.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 53] ﴿So it will be, and We will marry them to fair women with wide, beautiful eyes.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 54] ﴿They will call therein for every kind of fruit, secure.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 55] ﴿They will not taste therein death, except the first death; and He will protect them from the torment of Hellfire.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 56] ﴿As a bounty from your Lord. That is the great attainment.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 57] ﴿Indeed, We have made it easy in your tongue so that they may remember.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 58] ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 59].

When the Most High mentioned the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, He mentioned His favour to the Children of Israel, beginning with the averting of harm from them, which was their deliverance from the torment they had been in. Then He mentioned the continuing benefit to them, from His choosing them over the worlds and His giving them the signs. The humiliating torment was the killing of their sons and their employment in arduous labour. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ as ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ [the attributive construction], which is an idafa of the noun to its adjective, like بَقْلَةِ الحَمْقاءِ (the foolish herb, i.e., purslane). And ﴿مِن فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ is a substitute (badal, appositive substitute) for (مِنَ العَذابِ), with an omitted modifier, meaning "from the torment of Pharaoh." Then the modifier was omitted, and Pharaoh himself was made the torment, as hyperbole (mubalaghah). It was also said: it is connected to an omitted word, meaning "existing and proceeding from Pharaoh." When He described Pharaoh with severity and atrocity, He said: "Who is Pharaoh?", meaning: do you know him, who he is in his arrogance and rebellion? Then He made his state in that clear by saying ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ عالِيًا مِنَ المُسْرِفِينَ﴾ (Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors), meaning: exalted over the world, or arrogant, a transgressor among the transgressors.

﴿ولَقَدِ اخْتَرْناهُمْ﴾ means: We chose them and honoured them. (عَلى عِلْمٍ) — عِلْمٍ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) whose agent is not mentioned. It was said: "knowingly on their part and with excellence in them, so We chose them for prophethoods and messengerships." It was also said: "knowingly on Our part," meaning knowing the place of choice and that they deserved to be chosen. It was also said: "knowingly on Our part of what would proceed from them of justice, goodness, knowledge and faith, and that they would go astray and commit lapses in some matters."

(p. 38) It was also said: We chose them through this deliverance and these blessings, on account of prior knowledge We had of them, and We singled them out for that over the worlds. (عَلى العالَمِينَ): meaning the worlds of their own time, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to them. It was also said: "over the worlds" is general because of the large number of prophets among them, while this is specific to them and not to others. The choosing was from this aspect, since the community of Muhammad is superior. The word عَلى in His saying (عَلى عِلْمٍ) does not have the same meaning as عَلى in His saying (عَلى العالَمِينَ), and for this reason both were attached to a single verb, since the meaning differed, as in the poet's verse:

"And one day upon the back of the sand dune she became unattainable to me, and swore an oath that was not qualified."

So عَلى عِلْمٍ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), either from the agent or from the object. And عَلى ظَهْرِ is a circumstantial clause from the agent in تَعَذَّرَتْ, and the governing element (al-ʿāmil) of the one who has the circumstance is the verb.

﴿وآتَيْناهم مِنَ الآياتِ﴾ means: the manifest miracles among the people of Pharaoh, and what they were afflicted with, and among the Children of Israel what He bestowed upon them of shading by the clouds, manna and quails, and other things that He did not manifest to others.

﴿ما فِيهِ بَلاءٌ﴾ means: a clear test with blessings, or the trial through blessings, like His saying: ﴿ونَبْلُوكم بِالشَّرِّ والخَيْرِ﴾ (And We test you with evil and good) [al-Anbiya': 35]. (إنَّ هَؤُلاءِ): meaning the Quraysh, and in the demonstrative there is belittling of them.

﴿لَيَقُولُونَ﴾ ﴿إنْ هي إلّا مَوْتَتُنا الأُولى﴾ means: death is confined to our first death. He had said: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكم ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكم ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكُمْ﴾ (You were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life) [al-Baqarah: 28], mentioning two deaths, a first and a second. They denied that there would be a second death for them. The meaning is: the end of our affair and the limit of our existence is only at our death. Thus their statement implies the denial of resurrection. Then they stated explicitly what their statement implied, saying: ﴿وما نَحْنُ بِمُنْشَرِينَ﴾ (and we will not be resurrected), meaning: we will not be raised to everlasting life in which there is reckoning, reward and punishment. Their saying was in the sense of their saying: ﴿إنْ هي إلّا حَياتُنا الدُّنْيا وما نَحْنُ بِمَبْعُوثِينَ﴾ (There is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected) [al-An'am: 29].

﴿فَأْتُوا بِآبائِنا﴾: an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to the believers who were promising them resurrection, meaning: if you are truthful in what you say, then revive for us those of our sons who died, by asking your Lord, so that this would be a proof of resurrection in the Hereafter. It was said: they asked the Messenger to supplicate to Allah so that He would revive for them Quṣayy ibn Kilab, that they might consult him concerning the truth of prophethood and resurrection, since he was their elder and their consultant in calamities. (أهم): meaning the Quraysh, ﴿خَيْرٌ أمْ قَوْمُ تُبَّعٍ﴾? Apparently Tubba' is a well-known person, and comparison was made between his people and the people of the Messenger (ﷺ). Although the word Tubba' is applied to everyone who ruled the Arabs, just as Kisra is applied to whoever ruled Persia and Caesar to whoever ruled Rome. It was said: his name was As'ad al-Himyari, and he was called Abu Karib. Abu Hatim al-Riyashi mentioned that he believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) seven hundred years before he was sent. It is reported that when he believed in Medina, he wrote a letter and composed poetry. As for the poetry, it is:

"I bear witness concerning Ahmad that he is a messenger from Allah, Creator of souls."

"If my life were extended to his life, I would be his minister and his cousin."

As for the letter, Ibn Ishaq and others reported that it contained: "To proceed: I have believed in you and in the Book that was revealed to you, and I am upon your religion and your practice. I have believed in your Lord and the Lord of everything, and I have believed in everything that came from your Lord of the laws of Islam. If I attain you, then so be it, and how excellent; and if I do not attain you, then intercede for me and do not forget me on the Day of Resurrection, for I am of your first community. I followed you before your coming, and I am upon your creed and the creed of your father Abraham (peace be upon him)." Then he sealed the letter and engraved upon it: "To Allah belongs the command, before and after." He wrote its address: "To Muhammad son of ʿAbd Allah, the Prophet of Allah and His Messenger, the Seal of the Prophets, and the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds (ﷺ), from Tubba' the First." It is said that the letter and the poetry were with Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd, and they remained with him until the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, and they had been inheriting them generation after generation until they delivered them to the Prophet (ﷺ).

From Ibn ʿAbbas: Tubba' was a prophet. And from him: when Tubba' came from the East, after he had overcome al-Hira and Samarqand, he headed for Medina, having left behind some of his people there when he traveled, and they were killed by stealth, so he resolved to destroy it and exterminate its people. They gathered the Ansar for him and went out to fight him, and they would fight him by day and host him by night. This pleased him and he said: "Indeed, these people are noble." Then Ka'b and Asad, two cousins of Qurayzah, neighbours, came to him and informed him that "it will be prevented between you and what you want, for it is the migration place of a prophet from Quraysh named Muhammad, and his birthplace is in Mecca." Their statement turned him away from what he intended. Then they invited him to their religion, and he followed them and honoured them. They departed from Medina, and with them a group of Jews. On the way, a group from Hudhayl said to him: "We will guide you to a house in Mecca in which there is a treasure of pearls, chrysolite and silver." Hudhayl wanted his destruction, because they knew that no one who intended him harm would fail to perish. He mentioned this to the two rabbis, and they said: "We do not know of any house for Allah on earth other than this one. Take it as a place of worship, perform your sacrifice there, and shave your head. The people only intended your destruction." So he honoured it and covered it with cloth, and he was the first to clothe the House. He cut off the hands and feet of those men from Hudhayl, put out their eyes, and crucified them.

Some people said: by Tubba' is not meant a single man, but rather the kings of Yemen, who were called the Tababi'ah (tubba'ah). What appears is that he meant one of these, whom the Arabs know by this name more than others know it. In a hadith: "Do not revile Tubba', for he was a believer." This indicates that he is one specific person. Al-Jawhari said: the Tababi'ah are the kings of Yemen; and al-tubbaʿ is the shadow; and al-tubbaʿ is a kind of bird. Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli said: Tubba' is the title of every king of Yemen, al-Shihr and Hadramawt, and the king of Yemen alone is not called Tubba', as al-Mas'udi said. The comparison in which superiority is claimed concerns two categories, neither of which has goodness in them, relative to strength and power, as He said: ﴿أكُفّارُكم خَيْرٌ مِن أُولَئِكُمْ﴾ (Are your disbelievers better than those?) [al-Qamar: 43]. In Ibn ʿAbbas's exegesis, after mentioning the family of Pharaoh: "Are they stronger, or the people of Tubba'?" The attribution of "people" (qawm) to Tubba' is evidence that his creed was not theirs.

﴿أهْلَكْناهم إنَّهم كانُوا مُجْرِمِينَ﴾: a report of what He did to them, and an alert that the cause of destruction is criminality. In this there is a warning to the Quraysh and a threat that He may do to them what He did to the people of Tubba' and those before them, the deniers of the messengers, for their criminality. Then He mentioned the decisive proof of the correctness of the doctrine of resurrection, which is the creation of the world in truth. Most readers recite (وما بَيْنَهُما) with the masculine dual, but Ubayd ibn ʿUmayr read: (وما بَيْنَهُنَّ لاعِبِينَ). Muqatil said: "playing" means "frivolous."

﴿ما خَلَقْناهُما إلّا بِالحَقِّ﴾ means: with justice, rewarding the doer of good and the doer of evil with the reward and punishment He wills. (ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ): that He created that, so they do not fear punishment nor hope for reward. It has been recited مِيقاتَهم in the accusative, as the subject of إنَّ, with the predicate being يَوْمَ الفَصْلِ, meaning: indeed, the Day of Judgment is their appointed time and their recompense. ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُغْنِي مَوْلًى عَنْ مَوْلًى شَيْئًا﴾ encompasses all mawla (close ties, such as kinship, manumission, or allegiance) so that they avail nothing at all, meaning not even a little. (ولا هم يُنْصَرُونَ): plural, because مَوْلًى after the negation is general, so it returned to the meaning, not to the wording.

﴿إلّا مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾: al-Kisa'i said: مَن رَحِمَ is in the accusative as an disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ, an exception not of the same category), meaning: "but whom Allah has had mercy on, no one will be able to avail him of what they need from those whom He has cursed among the created." It was said that it is possible for the exception to be connected (istithnā' muttaṣil), meaning: no close relative avails another close relative, except the believers, for it will be permitted for them to intercede for one another. Al-Hawfi said: it may be a substitute (badal) for the nominative mawla, and yughnī would mean yanfaʿu (avails). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute for the waw in (يُنْصَرُونَ), meaning: none will prevent from the punishment except whom Allah has had mercy on, and al-Hawfi had said this before him.

﴿إنَّهُ هو العَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾: He does not help one who disobeyed Him; the Merciful to whoever obeys Him and to whom He pardons.

Then Ka'b and Asad, two cousins of Qurayzah, neighbours, came to him and informed him that "it will be prevented between you and what you want, for it is the migration place of a prophet from Quraysh named Muhammad, and his birthplace is in Mecca." Their statement turned him away from what he intended. Then they invited him to their religion, and he followed them and honoured them. They departed from Medina, and with them a group of Jews. On the way, a group from Hudhayl said to him: "We will guide you to a house in Mecca in which there is a treasure of pearls, chrysolite and silver." Hudhayl wanted his destruction, because they knew that no one who intended him harm would fail to perish. He mentioned this to the two rabbis, and they said: "We do not know of any house for Allah on earth other than this one. Take it as a place of worship, perform your sacrifice there, and shave your head. The people only intended your destruction." So he honoured it and covered it with cloth, and he was the first to clothe the House. He cut off the hands and feet of those men from Hudhayl, put out their eyes, and crucified them.

Some people said: by Tubba' is not meant a single man, but rather the kings of Yemen, who were called the Tababi'ah (tubba'ah). What appears is that he meant one of these, whom the Arabs know by this name more than others know it. In a hadith: "Do not revile Tubba', for he was a believer." This indicates that he is one specific person. Al-Jawhari said: the Tababi'ah are the kings of Yemen; and al-tubbaʿ is the shadow; and al-tubbaʿ is a kind of bird. Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli said: Tubba' is the title of every king of Yemen, al-Shihr and Hadramawt, and the king of Yemen alone is not called Tubba', as al-Mas'udi said. The comparison in which superiority is claimed concerns two categories, neither of which has goodness in them, relative to strength and power, as He said: ﴿أكُفّارُكم خَيْرٌ مِن أُولَئِكُمْ﴾ (Are your disbelievers better than those?) [al-Qamar: 43]. In Ibn ʿAbbas's exegesis, after mentioning the family of Pharaoh: "Are they stronger, or the people of Tubba'?" The attribution of "people" (qawm) to Tubba' is evidence that his creed was not theirs.

﴿أهْلَكْناهم إنَّهم كانُوا مُجْرِمِينَ﴾: a report of what He did to them, and an alert that the cause of destruction is criminality. In this there is a warning to the Quraysh and a threat that He may do to them what He did to the people of Tubba' and those before them, the deniers of the messengers, for their criminality. Then He mentioned the decisive proof of the correctness of the doctrine of resurrection, which is the creation of the world in truth. Most readers recite (وما بَيْنَهُما) with the masculine dual, but Ubayd ibn ʿUmayr read: (وما بَيْنَهُنَّ لاعِبِينَ). Muqatil said: "playing" means "frivolous."

﴿ما خَلَقْناهُما إلّا بِالحَقِّ﴾ means: with justice, rewarding the doer of good and the doer of evil with the reward and punishment He wills. (ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ): that He created that, so they do not fear punishment nor hope for reward. It has been recited مِيقاتَهم in the accusative, as the subject of إنَّ, with the predicate being يَوْمَ الفَصْلِ, meaning: indeed, the Day of Judgment is their appointed time and their recompense. ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُغْنِي مَوْلًى عَنْ مَوْلًى شَيْئًا﴾ encompasses all mawla (close ties, such as kinship, manumission, or allegiance) so that they avail nothing at all, meaning not even a little. (ولا هم يُنْصَرُونَ): plural, because مَوْلًى after the negation is general, so it returned to the meaning, not to the wording.

﴿إلّا مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾: al-Kisa'i said: مَن رَحِمَ is in the accusative as an disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ, an exception not of the same category), meaning: "but whom Allah has had mercy on, no one will be able to avail him of what they need from those whom He has cursed among the created." It was said that it is possible for the exception to be connected (istithnā' muttaṣil), meaning: no close relative avails another close relative, except the believers, for it will be permitted for them to intercede for one another. Al-Hawfi said: it may be a substitute (badal) for the nominative mawla, and yughnī would mean yanfaʿu (avails). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿مَن رَحِمَ اللَّهُ﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute for the waw in (يُنْصَرُونَ), meaning: none will prevent from the punishment except whom Allah has had mercy on, and al-Hawfi had said this before him.

﴿إنَّهُ هو العَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾: He does not help one who disobeyed Him; the Merciful to whoever obeys Him and to whom He pardons.

(p. 38)

﴿And We had certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment,﴾ ﴿from Pharaoh. Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors.﴾ ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds,﴾ ﴿and We gave them of the signs that contained a clear trial.﴾ ﴿Indeed, these people are saying,﴾ ﴿"There is not but our first death, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ ﴿So bring our forefathers, if you should be truthful.﴾ ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is the appointed time for them all,﴾ ﴿the Day when no close friend will avail another close friend at all, nor will they be aided,﴾ ﴿except those on whom Allah has mercy. Indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 43] ﴿is the food of the sinful.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 44] ﴿Like murky oil, it boils in the bellies,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 45] ﴿like the boiling of scalding water.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 46] ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of Hellfire.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 47] ﴿Then pour over his head the torment of scalding water.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 48] ﴿Taste it; indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 49] ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 50] ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 51] ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 52] ﴿wearing fine silk and brocade, facing one another.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 53] ﴿So it will be, and We will marry them to fair women with wide, beautiful eyes.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 54] ﴿They will call therein for every kind of fruit, secure.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 55] ﴿They will not taste therein death, except the first death; and He will protect them from the torment of Hellfire.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 56] ﴿As a bounty from your Lord. That is the great attainment.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 57] ﴿Indeed, We have made it easy in your tongue so that they may remember.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 58] ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting.﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 59].

When the Most High mentioned the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, He mentioned His favour to the Children of Israel, beginning with the averting of harm from them, which was their deliverance from the torment they had been in. Then He mentioned the continuing benefit to them, from His choosing them over the worlds and His giving them the signs. The humiliating torment was the killing of their sons and their employment in arduous labour. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ as ﴿مِنَ العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ [the attributive construction], which is an idafa of the noun to its adjective, like بَقْلَةِ الحَمْقاءِ (the foolish herb, i.e., purslane). And ﴿مِن فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ is a substitute (badal, appositive substitute) for (مِنَ العَذابِ), with an omitted modifier, meaning "from the torment of Pharaoh." Then the modifier was omitted, and Pharaoh himself was made the torment, as hyperbole (mubalaghah). It was also said: it is connected to an omitted word, meaning "existing and proceeding from Pharaoh." Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿مَن فِرْعَوْنُ﴾ (who is Pharaoh?). مَن is an interrogative: a subject (mubtada'), and فِرْعَوْنُ is its predicate. When He described Pharaoh with severity and atrocity, He said: "Who is Pharaoh?", meaning: do you know him, who he is in his arrogance and rebellion? Then He made his state in that clear by saying ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ عالِيًا مِنَ المُسْرِفِينَ﴾ (Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors), meaning: exalted over the world, or arrogant, a transgressor among the transgressors.

﴿ولَقَدِ اخْتَرْناهُمْ﴾ means: We chose them and honoured them. (عَلى عِلْمٍ) — عِلْمٍ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) whose agent is not mentioned. It was said: "knowingly on their part and with excellence in them, so We chose them for prophethoods and messengerships." It was also said: "knowingly on Our part," meaning knowing the place of choice and that they deserved to be chosen. It was also said: "knowingly on Our part of what would proceed from them of justice, goodness, knowledge and faith, and that they would go astray and commit lapses in some matters."

(p. 38) It was also said: We chose them through this deliverance and these blessings, on account of prior knowledge We had of them, and We singled them out for that over the worlds. (عَلى العالَمِينَ): meaning the worlds of their own time, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to them. It was also said: "over the worlds" is general because of the large number of prophets among them, while this is specific to them and not to others. The choosing was from this aspect, since the community of Muhammad is superior. The word عَلى in His saying (عَلى عِلْمٍ) does not have the same meaning as عَلى in His saying (عَلى العالَمِينَ), and for this reason both were attached to a single verb, since the meaning differed, as in the poet's verse:

"And one day upon the back of the sand dune she became unattainable to me, and swore an oath that was not qualified."

So عَلى عِلْمٍ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), either from the agent or from the object. And عَلى ظَهْرِ is a circumstantial clause from the agent in تَعَذَّرَتْ, and the governing element (al-ʿāmil) of the one who has the circumstance is the verb.

﴿وآتَيْناهم مِنَ الآياتِ﴾ means: the manifest miracles among the people of Pharaoh, and what they were afflicted with, and among the Children of Israel what He bestowed upon them of shading by the clouds, manna and quails, and other things that He did not manifest to others.

﴿ما فِيهِ بَلاءٌ﴾ means: a clear test with blessings, or the trial through blessings, like His saying: ﴿ونَبْلُوكم بِالشَّرِّ والخَيْرِ﴾ (And We test you with evil and good) [al-Anbiya': 35]. (إنَّ هَؤُلاءِ): meaning the Quraysh, and in the demonstrative there is belittling of them.

﴿لَيَقُولُونَ﴾ ﴿إنْ هي إلّا مَوْتَتُنا الأُولى﴾ means: death is confined to our first death. He had said: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكم ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكم ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكُمْ﴾ (You were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life) [al-Baqarah: 28], mentioning two deaths, a first and a second. They denied that there would be a second death for them. The meaning is: the end of our affair and the limit of our existence is only at our death. Thus their statement implies the denial of resurrection. Then they stated explicitly what their statement implied, saying: ﴿وما نَحْنُ بِمُنْشَرِينَ﴾ (and we will not be resurrected), meaning: we will not be raised to everlasting life in which there is reckoning, reward and punishment. Their saying was in the sense of their saying: ﴿إنْ هي إلّا حَياتُنا الدُّنْيا وما نَحْنُ بِمَبْعُوثِينَ﴾ (There is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected) [al-An'am: 29].

﴿فَأْتُوا بِآبائِنا﴾: an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to the believers who were promising them resurrection, meaning: if you are truthful in what you say, then revive for us those of our sons who died, by asking your Lord, so that this would be a proof of resurrection in the Hereafter. It was said: they asked the Messenger to supplicate to Allah so that He would revive for them Quṣayy ibn Kilab, that they might consult him concerning the truth of prophethood and resurrection, since he was their elder and their consultant in calamities. (أهم): meaning the Quraysh, ﴿خَيْرٌ أمْ قَوْمُ تُبَّعٍ﴾? Apparently Tubba' is a well-known person, and comparison was made between his people and the people of the Messenger (ﷺ). Although the word Tubba' is applied to everyone who ruled the Arabs, just as Kisra is applied to whoever ruled Persia and Caesar to whoever ruled Rome. It was said: his name was As'ad al-Himyari, and he was called Abu Karib. Abu Hatim al-Riyashi mentioned that he believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) seven hundred years before he was sent. It is reported that when he believed in Medina, he wrote a letter and composed poetry. As for the poetry, it is:

"I bear witness concerning Ahmad that he is a messenger from Allah, Creator of souls."

"If my life were extended to his life, I would be his minister and his cousin."

As for the letter, Ibn Ishaq and others reported that it contained: "To proceed: I have believed in you and in the Book that was revealed to you, and I am upon your religion and your practice. I have believed in your Lord and the Lord of everything, and I have believed in everything that came from your Lord of the laws of Islam. If I attain you, then so be it, and how excellent; and if I do not attain you, then intercede for me and do not forget me on the Day of Resurrection, for I am of your first community. I followed you before your coming, and I am upon your creed and the creed of your father Abraham (peace be upon him)." Then he sealed the letter and engraved upon it: "To Allah belongs the command, before and after." He wrote its address: "To Muhammad son of ʿAbd Allah, the Prophet of Allah and His Messenger, the Seal of the Prophets, and the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds (ﷺ), from Tubba' the First." It is said that the letter and the poetry were with Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd, and they remained with him until the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, and they had been inheriting them generation after generation until they delivered them to the Prophet (ﷺ).

From Ibn ʿAbbas: Tubba' was a prophet. And from him: when Tubba' came from the East, after he had overcome al-Hira and Samarqand, he headed for Medina, having left behind some of his people there when he traveled, and they were killed by stealth, so he resolved to destroy it and exterminate its people. They gathered the Ansar for him and went out to fight him, and they would fight him by day and host him by night. This pleased him and he said: "Indeed, these people are noble." Then Ka'b and Asad, two cousins of Qurayzah, neighbours, came to him and informed him that "it will be prevented between you and what you want, for it is the migration place of a prophet from Quraysh named Muhammad, and his birthplace is in Mecca." On the way, a group from Hudhayl said to him: "We will guide you to a house in Mecca in which there is a treasure of pearls, chrysolite and silver." Hudhayl wanted his destruction, because they knew that no one who intended him harm would fail to perish. He mentioned this to the two rabbis, and they said: "We do not know of any house for Allah on earth other than this one. Take it as a place of worship, perform your sacrifice there, and shave your head. The people only intended your destruction." So he honoured it and covered it with cloth, and he was the first to clothe the House. He cut off the hands and feet of those men from Hudhayl, put out their eyes, and crucified them.

[al-Qamar: 43]. In Ibn ʿAbbas's exegesis, after mentioning the family of Pharaoh: "Are they stronger, or the people of Tubba'?" The attribution of "people" (qawm) to Tubba' is evidence that his creed was not theirs.

In this there is a warning to the Quraysh and a threat that He may do to them what He did to the people of Tubba' and those before them, the deniers of the messengers, for their criminality. (ولا هم يُنْصَرُونَ): plural, because مَوْلًى after the negation is general, so it returned to the meaning, not to the wording.

﴿إنَّهُ هو العَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾: He does not help one who disobeyed Him; the Merciful to whoever obeys Him and to whom He pardons.

﴿إنَّ شَجَرَةَ الزَّقُّومِ﴾ (Indeed, the tree of zaqqum): it is read with a kasra on the shin (شِينِ). The discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Saffat.

﴿طَعامُ الأثِيمِ﴾ (is the food of the sinner): the word is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah, hyperbolic form), meaning one who commits many sins. It is also said of him: "athūm," which is likewise an intensive form. It was interpreted as "the polytheist" (al-mushrik). Yahya ibn Salam said: "one who earns sin." From Ibn Zaydan: "al-Athim here is Abu Jahl," and it was said: "al-Walid."

(كالمُهْلِ) (like molten metal, *al-muhl*): it is the sediment of oil, or molten silver, or molten copper, or the dregs of tar or pus. The first of these is attributed to Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas, and the last to Ibn Abbas. Al-Hasan said: "kal-mahl," with a fatḥah on the mim, which is a dialectal variant of it. From Ibn Mas'ud and also Ibn Abbas: *al-mahl* is what has been melted of gold, silver, iron or lead. Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Hasan, the two Ibns (Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin? — as the text lists "al-Ibnan"), and Hafs read ﴿يَغْلِي﴾ (yaghli, boils) with a *yā'*, meaning the food. ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Abu Razin, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, (p-٤٠) Ibn Muhaysin, Talhah, and al-Hasan in one narration, and the rest of the seven, read ﴿تَغْلِي﴾ (taghli, boils) with a *tā'*, meaning the tree.

﴿كَغَلْيِ الحَمِيمِ﴾ (like the boiling of scalding water): it is water heated until it gives off vapour from its boiling.

﴿خُذُوهُ فاعْتِلُوهُ﴾ (Seize him and drag him): it is said to the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniyah): "Seize him and drag him," that is, drive him with violence and pulling. Al-A'mash said: the meaning of *i'tilūhu* is: break him as wood is broken, into the midst of the Blazing Fire (sawā' al-jaḥīm). Ibn Abbas said: its middle. Al-Hasan said: its greatest part. The majority read ﴿فاعْتِلُوهُ﴾ (i'tilūhu) with a kasra on the *tā'*; Zayd ibn Ali, the two Ibns, and Nafi' read it with a ḍammah, and there is disagreement on this from al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-A'raj and Abu Amr.

﴿ثُمَّ صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ مِن عَذابِ الحَمِيمِ﴾ (Then pour over his head some of the torment of scalding water): and in al-Hajj: ﴿يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمُ الحَمِيمُ﴾ (Scalding water will be poured over their heads) [al-Hajj: 19]. The thing actually poured is the scalding water, so at times the literal sense (al-ḥaqīqah) is considered, and at times the metaphor (al-isti'ārah) is considered, because it is more severe than the scalding water: what was poured is what results from it of pains and torment. So he expressed the effect (al-musabbab) by the cause (al-sabab), since torment is the effect of the scalding water. The word "torment" is more terrifying and more awe-inspiring.

﴿ذُقْ﴾ (Taste!): that is, the torment. ﴿إنَّكَ أنْتَ العَزِيزُ الكَرِيمُ﴾ (Indeed you were the mighty, the noble). This is said in mockery and derision toward one who used to exalt himself and act nobly among his people. From Qatadah: when the verses ﴿إنَّ شَجَرَةَ الزَّقُّومِ﴾ ﴿طَعامُ الأثِيمِ﴾ were revealed, Abu Jahl said: "Do you threaten me, O Muhammad? Between its two lava plains (lābatayhā) there is no one mightier or more noble than I." Then this verse was revealed, and at its end: ﴿ذُقْ إنَّكَ أنْتَ العَزِيزُ الكَرِيمُ﴾, that is, according to your claim. This is like what Jarir said:

Did you not, in the ruins you once inscribed with them, have one who was an admonition, O flower of Yemen?

He says it to a poet who named himself with it in his saying:

Convey to Kulayb, and convey on your behalf to its poet: I am the mightiest, and I am the flower of Yemen.

So Jarir brought it in the manner of mockery. It was also read: ﴿إنَّكَ﴾ with a kasra on the hamzah.
