The first of these is attributed to Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas, and the last to Ibn Abbas. Al-Hasan said: "kal-mahl," with a fatḥah on the mim, which is a dialectal variant of it. From Ibn Mas'ud and also Ibn Abbas: *al-mahl* is what has been melted of gold, silver, iron or lead. Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Hasan, the two Ibns (Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin? — as the text lists "al-Ibnan"), and Hafs read ﴿يَغْلِي﴾ (yaghli, boils) with a *yā'*, meaning the food. ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Abu Razin, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, (p-٤٠) Ibn Muhaysin, Talhah, and al-Hasan in one narration, and the rest of the seven, read ﴿تَغْلِي﴾ (taghli, boils) with a *tā'*, meaning the tree.

﴿كَغَلْيِ الحَمِيمِ﴾ (like the boiling of scalding water): it is water heated until it gives off vapour from its boiling.

﴿خُذُوهُ فاعْتِلُوهُ﴾ (Seize him and drag him): it is said to the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniyah): "Seize him and drag him," that is, drive him with violence and pulling. Al-A'mash said: the meaning of *i'tilūhu* is: break him as wood is broken, into the midst of the Blazing Fire (sawā' al-jaḥīm). Ibn Abbas said: its middle. Al-Hasan said: its greatest part. The majority read ﴿فاعْتِلُوهُ﴾ (i'tilūhu) with a kasra on the *tā'*; Zayd ibn Ali, the two Ibns, and Nafi' read it with a ḍammah, and there is disagreement on this from al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-A'raj and Abu Amr.

﴿ثُمَّ صُبُّوا فَوْقَ رَأْسِهِ مِن عَذابِ الحَمِيمِ﴾ (Then pour over his head some of the torment of scalding water): and in al-Hajj: ﴿يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمُ الحَمِيمُ﴾ (Scalding water will be poured over their heads) [al-Hajj: 19]. The thing actually poured is the scalding water, so at times the literal sense (al-ḥaqīqah) is considered, and at times the metaphor (al-isti'ārah) is considered, because it is more severe than the scalding water: what was poured is what results from it of pains and torment. So he expressed the effect (al-musabbab) by the cause (al-sabab), since torment is the effect of the scalding water. The word "torment" is more terrifying and more awe-inspiring.

﴿ذُقْ﴾ (Taste!): that is, the torment. ﴿إنَّكَ أنْتَ العَزِيزُ الكَرِيمُ﴾ (Indeed you were the mighty, the noble). This is said in mockery and derision toward one who used to exalt himself and act nobly among his people. From Qatadah: when the verses ﴿إنَّ شَجَرَةَ الزَّقُّومِ﴾ ﴿طَعامُ الأثِيمِ﴾ were revealed, Abu Jahl said: "Do you threaten me, O Muhammad? Between its two lava plains (lābatayhā) there is no one mightier or more noble than I." Then this verse was revealed, and at its end: ﴿ذُقْ إنَّكَ أنْتَ العَزِيزُ الكَرِيمُ﴾, that is, according to your claim. This is like what Jarir said:

Did you not, in the ruins you once inscribed with them, have one who was an admonition, O flower of Yemen?

He says it to a poet who named himself with it in his saying:

Convey to Kulayb, and convey on your behalf to its poet: I am the mightiest, and I am the flower of Yemen.

So Jarir brought it in the manner of mockery. It was also read: ﴿إنَّكَ﴾ with a kasra on the hamzah. Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib read it from the pulpit, and al-Kisa'i with a fatḥah: ﴿أنَّ هَذا﴾ (that this), that is, the matter or the torment, ﴿ما كُنْتُمْ بِهِ تَمْتَرُونَ﴾ (which you used to doubt), that is, you used to dispute it. When he mentioned the state of the disbelievers, he followed it with the state of the believers, saying: ﴿إنَّ المُتَّقِينَ في مَقامٍ أمِينٍ﴾ (Indeed the God-fearing will be in a secure place). Abdullah ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Nafi', and Ibn Amir read ﴿في مُقامٍ﴾ (muqām) with a ḍammah on the mim; Abu Raja', Isa, Yahya, al-A'mash, and the rest of the seven read it with a fatḥah. He described the place (al-maqām) as "secure" (amīn), that is, one is kept safe in it from others. So it is as if it is a faʿīl in the sense of a maf'ūl, that is, "entrusted," meaning one is safe in it. This was said by Ibn Atiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: "amīn" is from your saying: "the man was secure (amanah), so he is amīn," and it is the opposite of "khā'in" (treacherous). So it is described with it as a metaphor (isti'ārah), because a frightening place used to frighten its occupant with what he encounters in it of hardships. The explanation of *al-sundus* and *al-istabraq* has already passed. Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿وإسْتَبْرَقٍ﴾ (wa-istabraqin) as a past verb (fi'l māḍī), making it a verb. ﴿مُتَقابِلِينَ﴾ (facing one another) is a description of the sittings of the people of Paradise, so that none of them turns his back on another in the gatherings. ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ (thus): that is, the matter is so. The majority read ﴿بِحُورٍ﴾ (with wide-eyed maidens), with tanwīn, and ʿIkrimah without tanwīn, because the "ʿīn" (dark-eyed ones) are divided into ḥūr and non-ḥūr, so these are of the ḥūr al-ʿīn, not of, for example, the shahlan (grey-eyed ones).

﴿يَدْعُونَ فِيها﴾ (They will call for therein): that is, the servants and those who attend to them, ﴿بِكُلِّ فاكِهَةٍ﴾ (for every kind of fruit), they wish to have it brought to them. (آمِنِينَ) (secure) from illnesses and indigestion.

﴿لا يَذُوقُونَ فِيها المَوْتَ﴾ (They will not taste death therein). ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read: *lā yudhāqūna* (they will not be made to taste), in the passive voice.

﴿إلّا المَوْتَةَ الأُولى﴾ (except the first death): this is a disconnected exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ, an exception not from the same category), meaning: but the first death, they tasted it in the world. This is a reminder of the everlasting immortality that He has bestowed upon them, and a reminder to them of departing from the transient world to this lasting abode. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how is the first death, which was tasted before entering Paradise, excluded from the negated death? I say: the intention is that it be said: "they will not taste death in it at all," so the phrase ﴿إلّا المَوْتَةَ الأُولى﴾ is placed in the position of that, because the past death cannot be tasted in the future, for they will taste it (in the past). Ibn Atiyyah said: some people took *illā* (except) to mean *siwā* (other than), and al-Tabari weakened that and took it to mean *baʿda* (after), but his weakening is not correct; rather the meaning holds and is consistent with *siwā*. As for the meaning of the verse, it is clear that it negates for them the tasting of death, and that nothing of that reaches them except what preceded in the world. Abu Haywah read ﴿ووَقّاهم﴾ (wa-waqqāhum, and He protected them), with shaddah on the qāf. The pronoun in ﴿يَسَّرْناهُ﴾ (We have made it easy) refers to the Qur'an; ﴿بِلِسانِكَ﴾ (in your tongue) means in your language, which is the language of the Arabs.

(p-٤١) (fārtaqib, so wait) for the victory which We promised you. ﴿إنَّهم مُرْتَقِبُونَ﴾ (Indeed they too are waiting) for the reversals (al-dawā'ir) against you, according to what they suppose. In it there is a promise for him, peace be upon him, a warning for them, and a relinquishing (mutārakah) that has been abrogated (mansūkhah, abrogated by naskh) by the verses of the sword (āyāt al-sayf).
